title: Euenius · lines 41–49
subtitle: Wolves kill sixty of the sacred sheep while Euenius sleeps; he tries to hide the loss, and the Apollonians blind him

units.en: Once, when he had fallen asleep, wolves got into the cave and killed about sixty of the sheep.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.body: The guard falls asleep on duty, so the reader sees Euenius fail at the very task he was chosen for.

notes.label: Juxtaposition
notes.body: The sleeping guard is placed right next to the wolves, so danger arrives the moment he drops off.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.body: A participle and a verb tell the whole attack in two words, so it happens as suddenly as it would in reality.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The number comes last in the sentence, which brings home the size of the loss.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.trans: he kept quiet and told no one
notes.body: The same idea is said twice, positively and negatively, which shows that the cover-up is deliberate.

notes.label: Emphatic negative
notes.body: "No one" is a strong word, which shows he told absolutely nobody.

notes.label: Characterisation
notes.trans: to replace them by buying others
notes.body: Euenius thinks sacred animals can simply be bought and swapped, which shows his lack of respect for the gods.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The story switches from Euenius alone to the whole city, which sets one man against his community.

notes.label: Litotes
notes.body: An understatement that means they knew perfectly well, so his cover-up looks hopeless from the start.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.trans: they took him to court and condemned him
notes.body: Trial and verdict are packed into one participle and one verb, which makes the city's justice seem hasty.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The punishment comes at the very end of the sentence, so the reader is struck by its cruelty.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: The Apollonians punish Euenius but bring suffering on themselves, so the reader suspects they were wrong.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The blight follows the blinding at once, so the reader links the two even before the oracle explains it.

notes.label: Parallelism
notes.quote: οὔτε πρόβατα … ἔτικτεν οὔτε γῆ ἔφερεν
notes.trans: neither did the sheep bear … nor did the land yield
notes.body: Two matching clauses cover both flocks and fields, which shows that the whole community is suffering.

questions: Was Euenius' real offence falling asleep, or what he did afterwards? Use the Greek to support your answer.
